mainEntity.name: How long should sensitivity last after a new crown?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some degree of sensitivity following crown placement is a normal part of the adjustment period. Most patients find that sensitivity to temperature or pressure settles within one to two weeks as the tooth and surrounding gum tissue adapt. If sensitivity is significant, does not improve after two weeks, or becomes worse over time, it is advisable to contact your dental practice. Your dentist can check whether the bite alignment is correct, assess the gum tissue, and determine whether any further action is appropriate for your individual situation.

mainEntity.name: Can I eat normally straight after having a crown fitted?

acceptedAnswer.text: After a permanent crown is fitted, your dentist will usually advise you to wait until any local anaesthetic has fully worn off before eating. This reduces the risk of inadvertently biting your cheek or tongue. For the first 24–48 hours, it is generally recommended to eat softer foods and avoid the crowned side where possible. Temporary crowns require more caution — sticky and hard foods should be avoided throughout the temporary phase to reduce the risk of displacement.

mainEntity.name: Is it normal for a crown to feel different when biting?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is quite common for a newly placed crown to feel slightly different to your natural bite. Your teeth and jaw will often adjust naturally within a few days. However, if the crown consistently feels too high when you close your teeth, or if biting causes notable discomfort, this may indicate that a minor bite adjustment is needed. This is a straightforward procedure that your dentist can perform at a short follow-up appointment. Do not delay contacting your dental practice if bite discomfort continues.

mainEntity.name: Can decay still develop under a dental crown?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — decay can develop at the margin where the crown meets the natural tooth, particularly if oral hygiene in this area is inadequate. The crown material itself cannot decay, but the natural tooth structure beneath and around the crown remains susceptible to bacterial acid. This is why maintaining effective cleaning at and around the crown margin — including flossing or using interdental brushes — is so important. Regular dental check-ups also allow your dentist to monitor the crown margins for early signs of change. For concerns about recurrent sensitivity or hidden decay risk, this guide on whether a tooth under a crown can still get a cavity offers additional context.

mainEntity.name: What should I do if my crown falls out?

acceptedAnswer.text: If your crown comes out, remain calm. Rinse the crown gently with clean water and store it somewhere safe — ideally in a small container or a sealed bag. Avoid attempting to re-cement it yourself using household adhesives, as these can be harmful to oral tissues and may interfere with professional re-cementation. Contact your dental practice as soon as possible to arrange an appointment. In many cases, a crown can be re-cemented, though your dentist will examine the tooth and crown to assess whether this is appropriate.

mainEntity.name: How long should a dental crown last?

acceptedAnswer.text: The lifespan of a dental crown depends on a number of factors including the material used, the position of the tooth in the mouth, your oral hygiene habits, and whether you grind your teeth. Crowns that are well maintained and regularly reviewed can last ten years or longer in many cases, though it is not possible to guarantee a specific lifespan for any individual restoration. Your dentist can give you an indication of what to expect based on your particular crown and oral health circumstances.
